title: Waypoint — plan trips with your agent, beside you
pitch: A trip planner where your AI agent works INSIDE the page with you — visible, constrained by your 🔒 locks, and corrected by the app's own math
about_excerpt: A trip planner where your AI agent works INSIDE the page with you — visible, constrained by your 🔒 locks, and corrected by the app's own math Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Trip planners are single-player, and AI travel agents that book through a backend leave your screen behind — the agent works on a hidden copy of your data while you stare at a chat window. We wanted the third model: an AI agent that works INSIDE the page, beside you — visible, correctable, and constrained by your decisions. WebMCP made that possible, so we built Waypoint for The WebMCP Challenge. What it does Waypoint is a trip itinerary planner where you plan in the UI and an AI agent (ChatGPT desktop's built-in browser) works on the same board through 8 tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() : The agent reads the itinerary, adds/updates/removes activities, re-orders days, audits conflicts and budget. You keep hard control: activities you 🔒-lock are enforced in the tool contract — reorder_day refuses to move them and explains why. The agent literally cannot touch your locked lunch. The app does the math, the agent does the judgment: overlap detection and budget totals are computed deterministically and returned as JSON from every mutation, so the agent verifies its own changes in one turn. A shared activity feed logs every human and agent action — you watch your agent work beside you. In the demo video, the human resets the board mid-session, the conflict reappears, and the agent catches it and fixes it live on screen — leaving the locked lunch untouched. How we built it React 18 + TypeScript + Vite 6 + Tailwind v4 — a static site with zero backend and zero API keys : the browsing agent is the AI. src/webmcp.ts registers all 8 tools per the WebMCP spec , with JSON-Schema inputs and agent-oriented JSON returns (post-change schedule + new conflicts + budget deltas + actionable hints). Both WebMCP APIs in one app: set_trip_budget is also a real HTML <form> carrying the spec's proposed declarative attributes ( toolname / tooldescription / toolparamdescription / toolautosubmit ). Flag-enabled Chrome auto-registers the form as a tool — we watched it happen ("Duplicate tool name" was the happy error). An in-app agent simulator executes the identical tool implementations, so visitors without a WebMCP browser still experience the collaboration. State lives in a pure reducer + localStorage; tool mutations apply synchronously so a tool's return value always reflects its own change. Deployed on GitHub Pages; the Devpost video's voiceover is Deepgram TTS and the edit was scripted with ffmpeg. Challenges we ran into Chrome 152 expired the #enable-webmcp-testing flag — "Enabled" was a silent no-op until we also enabled the "Temporarily unexpire M150/M151 flags". Then "modelContext" in document returned true and all 8 tools registered. ChatGPT's regular chat only "searches" pages — Site tools attach only in the desktop app's built-in browser with Codex/Work (on GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra). Finding that flow took real debugging. A sneaky HTML5 validation bug: the budget form had step=5 + min=1 , silently rejecting round numbers like 150 — caught only because we functionally tested every form before recording. Hosting hurdles: a leftover CNAME in a GitHub user-pages repo was redirecting all our Pages URLs, and Git Bash mangled Vite's --base=/WebPoint/ into Program Files/Git/WebPoint/ on the first deploy. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full human + agent loop works end-to-end in the judges' environment: green "WebMCP live" chip, agent fixing conflicts live on screen, lock refusals, budget checks — verified, not mocked. The collaboration contract (human locks as tool-enforced constraints, app-returned math) is implemented exactly as designed. What we learned WebMCP flips the integration model: instead of the agent bypassing your UI, your UI becomes the agent's API — and that makes human control a schema-level feature , not a hope. Returning rich post-state from mutating tools lets agents self-correct in one round trip. Test the boring paths (HTML forms!) as hard as the shiny ones. What's next Multi-trip support and shared trips (multiple humans + agents on one board). A lock-approval flow: agent proposes, human accepts — one click at a time. Shipping a small "site tools" badge pattern other sites can copy.
